Ring slots are 16-byte aligned and densely packed. 22: - **Reactive emission**: only the nodes that changed emit opcodes. 440: ## Reactive Emission
441: 
442: The engine emits **only what changed** relative to its previous emission:
443: 
444: - **Property diff**: a changed `spacing`/`padding`/`WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`ALIGNMENT`/
445:   text emits a single `SET_PROPERTY` / `SET_TEXT` for that node. (Padding is a
446:   styling modifier, but it still diffs and emits like any other property.)
447: - **Structural diff**: a node added/removed/moved emits the corresponding
448:   `TREE` opcode(s).
449: - **Steady state**: an unchanged tree emits **zero** opcodes.
450: 
451: The **`frame` compound modifier** (width/height/alignment) is not a distinct
452: protocol concept: it emits `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`/`ALIGNMENT` as ordinary
453: `PARAMETER:SET_PROPERTY` deltas, exactly like any other constraint property. There
454: is no `frame` opcode or dedicated wire type.
455: 
456: Signals in the application drive this: a signal marks the tree dirty; the
457: engine's next `emit` reconciles and writes only the delta. The renderer applies
458: each frame as a delta to its native elements.

462: ## Linear Memory Layout
463: 
464: The guest engine and host share a **single linear memory**. Regions are fixed at module start:
465: 
466: ```
467: +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
468: | 0x0000  Header block (80 B)  — cursors, frame counter, layout  |
469: | 0x0050  Ring buffer (16 B × slotCount)   [guest → host]        |
470: | ...      (slots densely packed, 64-byte aligned base)          |
471: | 0x10050 Event ring buffer (16 B × slotCount) [host → guest]    |
472: | ...                                                           |
473: | 0x20050 Arena (bump region, guest-owned: strings / tokens)     |
474: | ...                                                           |
475: | 0x30050 Event arena (bump region, host-owned: event strings)   |
476: | ...                                                            |
477: +───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────+
478: ```
479: 
480: > The event ring is the **host → guest** direction of the shared-memory
481: > transport: the renderer writes `EVENT`-category opcodes here and the
482: > guest/app drains them. It uses the same 16-byte slot layout as the main
483: > (guest → host) ring; both share `slotCount` (same capacity).
484: >
485: > The **event arena** is the host-owned bump region that makes strings flow
486: > **host → guest** over the shared ring: a renderer bump-allocates `TEXT_CHANGED`
487: > text (and any future string-bearing event payload) here and references it by
488: > its absolute byte offset — exactly mirroring how the guest uses the guest
489: > arena for `SET_TEXT` / STRING properties. The host resets its cursor on
490: > `META::RESET`; if the event arena is full the host applies backpressure
491: > (drops/stalls the event), mirroring ring backpressure.

517: ### Ring buffer
518: 
519: - Contiguous array of **16-byte slots**; `slotCount` is a **power of two** (wrap via mask, no modulo).
520: - **Producer** (guest) writes at `writeCursor`, then advances `writeCursor` and increments `frameCount` at frame end.
521: - **Consumer** (host) reads from `readCursor` up to `writeCursor`; after draining a frame it advances `readCursor`.
522: - **Backpressure**: the producer must not advance `writeCursor` past `readCursor` (ring full). The producer SHOULD flush a frame before the ring is full.
523: - **Frame boundary detection**: the host watches `frameCount`. When it advances, exactly one frame (all slots from the previously consumed `readCursor` to the current `writeCursor`) is complete.
524: 
525: ### Event ring (host → guest)
526: 
527: - The **host** (renderer) is the producer: it writes `EVENT`-category opcodes at `eventWriteCursor`.
528: - The **guest** (app/engine) is the consumer: it reads from `eventReadCursor` up to `eventWriteCursor`, then advances `eventReadCursor`.
529: - Events are raw inputs and are consumed as soon as they are written (no frame batching); `eventFrameCount` is not required.
530: - Backpressure mirrors the main ring: the host must not advance `eventWriteCursor` past `eventReadCursor`.
531: 
532: ### Arena
533: 
534: - A pre-allocated **bump region** for variable-length data (strings, token paths).
535: - Every arena entry is **self-describing**: `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]`.
536: - Opcodes reference entries by their **byte offset** (`arenaRef`), so an entry's length is read directly from the arena — all opcodes stay 16 bytes.
537: - The guest advances `arenaCursor` monotonically (no free-list, no fragmentation). The arena MAY be reset via `META::RESET`.
538: 
539: ### Event arena (host → guest)
540: 
541: The event arena is the **host-owned mirror** of the arena, giving the shared-memory
542: transport a host → guest string section so strings flow **both ways on all
543: transports**:

545: - The **host** (renderer) bump-allocates event string payloads here (e.g. the
546:   new text of a `TEXT_CHANGED`) and references them by their **absolute byte
547:   offset** in the event opcode — the same `SET_TEXT` shared-memory convention
548:   used in the guest arena.
549: - The **guest** resolves the text from the event arena region when draining
550:   events (`EVENT::TEXT_CHANGED`).
551: - Entries share the same self-describing `[u32 byteLength][bytes...]` layout as
552:   the guest arena.
553: - The host advances `eventArenaCursor` monotonically and resets it on
554:   `META::RESET`; a full event arena is backpressure (the host drops/stalls the
555:   event until the guest drains or a reset lands).
556: - Over the **network**, host → guest string payloads use the batch's string
557:   section with *relative* offsets instead (see [Transport](#transport)) — the
558:   same dual absolute/relative convention as `SET_TEXT`.

573: ## Design Token System
574: 
575: ### Core Principle
576: 
577: > **The application owns the theme. The renderer owns the defaults, the scheme
578: > detection, and the interaction states.**
579: 
580: - The **application** declares a theme: token overrides (base = **light**
581:   design, `dark.`-prefixed = **dark** design) and token references in style
582:   properties.
583: - The **renderer** supplies platform-appropriate defaults, derives the
584:   effective color scheme from the platform, resolves token references, and
585:   owns hover/pressed/focus/disabled styling.
586: 
587: This ensures a native look-and-feel by default and cross-platform consistency
588: when the application rolls a theme.
589: 
590: ### Tokens & color schemes
591: 
592: - Tokens are identified by **dot-separated string paths** (`color.primary`,
593:   `font.body.size`, `space.2`), case-sensitive, lowercase recommended. The
594:   `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type (`0x08`) references a token path stored in the
595:   arena; `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides a token's value globally.
596: - **Base = light. `dark.`-prefixed paths are the dark variant** (`dark.color.primary`).
597:   The renderer derives the effective scheme (light/dark) from the platform and
598:   re-resolves when it changes — scheme selection is never carried by the
599:   protocol.
600: - The **standard token catalog** (colors, typography, spacing, radii,
601:   elevations, `control.*`, per-component tokens) and the **resolution
602:   algorithm** (dark layer → override → default → parent → fallback) are defined
603:   in **[TOKENS.md](./TOKENS.md)**.
604: 
605: ### References in properties
606: 
607: Any property whose value type is `COLOR` / `F32` / `STRING` / `ENUM` MAY instead
608: carry the **`DESIGN_TOKEN`** value type (`0x08`), with `C` = arenaRef to the
609: token path. The renderer resolves the reference against the token tables and the
610: current scheme. A property carries exactly one value — a literal or a token
611: reference, never both. Because overrides and the scheme are renderer state, a
612: token-typed property requires **no re-emission** when a token changes.
613: 
614: ### Renderer Responsibilities
615: 
616: The renderer MUST:
617: 
618: 1. Provide platform-appropriate **light and dark defaults** for all Tier 1 tokens.
619: 2. Accept `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` commands and store overrides.
620: 3. Derive the effective color scheme from the platform and re-resolve on change.
621: 4. Resolve token references (`DESIGN_TOKEN` value type) in properties.
622: 5. Fall back to defaults when no override exists.
623: 6. Never transmit visual styling rules in the protocol.
624: 
625: The application MAY override any token via `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` (base and `dark.*`)
626: and reference tokens via the `DESIGN_TOKEN` value type; it MUST NOT assume
627: specific default token values. Tokens a renderer cannot apply are ignored (the
628: same "allowed and ignored" rule as unapplicable modifiers).

632: ## Frame Lifecycle
633: 
634: A frame is a batch of delta opcodes produced by one `emit` pass:
635: 
636: 1. Guest begins a frame.
637: 2. Guest emits the delta opcodes (tree structure and/or property changes) into consecutive ring slots.
638: 3. Guest allocates strings in the arena as needed.
639: 4. Guest `end_frame()`: publishes `writeCursor`, then increments `frameCount`.
640: 5. Host observes `frameCount` change, drains `[readCursor, writeCursor)`, advances `readCursor`.
641: 
642: Because the ring and arena are plain memory, the guest publishes via a single release store of `frameCount`; the host acquires on read.
643: 
644: ---
645: 
646: ## Transport
647: 
648: The opcode protocol is transport-agnostic. Two peer backends carry frames from
649: producer (guest engine) to consumer (host renderer):
650: 
651: | Backend | Scenario | Mechanism |
652: |---------|----------|-----------|
653: | Shared memory | Desktop / native (guest + host share linear memory) | The ring buffer + arena above; zero-copy |
654: | Network batch | SSR → browser (guest and host do **not** share memory) | Serialized batches of opcodes + arena delta |
655: 
656: The `Frame` type is the **transport seam**: a consumer (renderer) applies a
657: frame the same way whether it came from the shared-memory ring or a decoded
658: network batch.
659: 
660: ### Network batch format
661: 
662: ```
663: [u32 magic "PLPL"] [u16 version] [u16 flags] [u32 sequence] [u32 opcodeCount]
664: [opcode × opcodeCount (16 B each)]
665: [u32 arenaDeltaLen] [arena delta bytes]
666: ```
667: 
668: - **magic / version**: `0x504C504C` (`PLPL`, little-endian on the wire) / `1`.
669:   A decoder MUST reject batches with a mismatched magic or version.
670: - **flags**: direction. `0x0000` = guest → host (tree/style). Bit `0x0001` =
671:   host → guest (raw-input events); host → guest batches carry their string
672:   payloads in the batch's string section.
673: - **sequence**: a **per-stream monotonic message sequence** — the producer
674:   increments it by exactly one for each batch it encodes (guest → host delta
675:   batches only; heartbeat/request batches carry `0`). It is the network
676:   transport's loss detector; see [Sequence gap detection](#sequence-gap-detection).
677:   It is **not** the ring header's `frameCount` (a per-frame publish watermark
678:   for shared memory): opcodes from several emit-pass frames may coalesce into
679:   one batch, so a batch is the network unit, not a frame.
680: - **arena delta**: the bytes appended to the bump arena since the previous
681:   batch. The consumer keeps a **mirrored arena** and appends each delta, so
682:   absolute `arenaRef` offsets stay valid — identical to shared memory.
683: - **META::RESET**: a batch containing a reset opcode clears the consumer's
684:   mirrored arena before appending (offsets restart at 0).
685: 
686: ### Batching policy
687: 
688: The producer buffers opcodes and flushes a batch when **either** threshold is
689: reached (first trigger wins):
690: 
691: - **Time**: the interval since the first buffered opcode elapses (default **4 ms**).
692: - **Size**: the accumulated batch reaches a network-frame size (default **1400 bytes**).
693: 
694: Both thresholds are configurable; a producer MAY flush eagerly (e.g. on the
695: first frame after connection).
696: 
697: ### Sequence gap detection
698: 
699: The network backend is reliable and ordered **within a connection**, but a
700: middlebox can drop a batch while the socket stays "open", and a producer's send
701: path can wedge — either way the consumer silently misses deltas. The batch
702: `sequence` makes that loss detectable:
703: 
704: - **Producer**: maintain one monotonic `sequence` per stream, incremented by
705:   exactly one for **each encoded batch**. Only guest → host delta batches
706:   consume a sequence number; heartbeat (`META::PING`/`PONG`) and request
707:   batches (`META::RESYNC`, `META::ENVIRONMENT`, events) carry `0` and never
708:   advance it.
709: - **Consumer**: the first guest → host batch establishes a baseline
710:   (`expected = sequence + 1`). Every later guest → host batch MUST satisfy
711:   `sequence == expected`; then `expected = sequence + 1`. A batch whose
712:   sequence does not match means one or more batches were lost.
713: - **Recovery**: on a gap the consumer MUST NOT apply the gapped batch (its
714:   deltas assume the lost state) and MUST request a full snapshot
715:   (`META::RESYNC`), then re-baseline on the next guest → host batch. The
716:   consumer also re-baselines on every (re)connect.
717: - **Heartbeat batches are exempt**: a `META::PONG` (host → guest) is not part of
718:   the guest → host stream; consumers track only guest → host batches.
719: 
720: The recovery is **always a full snapshot**, never retransmission: the renderer
721: is stateless and the application owns the retained tree, so a `META::RESYNC`
722: reconverges the consumer regardless of what was lost. **Acknowledgements and a
723: retransmit queue are deliberately not part of the protocol** — they would add a
724: per-session send buffer and an ack exchange to a design whose recovery is
725: already a stateless snapshot.
726: 
727: ### Transport heartbeat
728: 
729: The **network batch backend** (a WebSocket / streamed connection) can fail
730: silently: a proxy or load balancer may drop the connection without a close
731: frame, or the peer's send path may wedge, leaving the socket "open" while
732: nothing is delivered. Neither side can detect this from the batch stream alone.
733: The heartbeat is the transport-liveness mechanism for this backend:
734: 
735: - **Probe**: the guest (client) sends a `META::PING` batch at a fixed cadence
736:   (default **every 5 s**). `A/B/C = 0`, no string section.
737: - **Reply**: the host (server) MUST answer each `META::PING` with a `META::PONG`
738:   batch as promptly as its send path allows.
739: - **Liveness**: a peer's *liveness* is any received batch — deltas, `PONG`, or
740:   anything else. A guest that receives no batch for **more than two probe
741:   intervals** SHOULD treat the connection as dead: close it and reconnect (the
742:   reconnect flow already re-syncs via `META::RESYNC`).
743: - **Host-side detection**: a host MAY additionally send WebSocket-protocol-level
744:   ping frames (browsers auto-answer) to detect a dead client and keep
745:   middleboxes from timing the connection out; a host whose send fails (or a
746:   probe that is never answered) SHOULD close the connection so the client
747:   reconnects instead of stalling.
748: - **Scope**: the heartbeat is **transport liveness only, NOT app state**. A
749:   `META::PING`/`META::PONG` batch MUST NOT be routed into the application — it
750:   never touches the retained tree, signals, or events. The **shared-memory ring
751:   backend MUST NOT use it**: ring peers are co-located and their liveness is the
752:   host process's concern, so the ring never carries, expects, or relays
753:   `META::PING`/`META::PONG`.
754:

1: # Pathland Conformance Test Vectors
2: 
3: **Wire protocol version:** 1
4: **Encoding:** little-endian
5: **Opcode size:** 16 bytes
6: 
7: This document provides **golden byte arrays** for the Pathland opcode protocol (see [OPCODE.md](./OPCODE.md)). A conforming implementation MUST:
8: 
9: - encode each opcode to exactly these 16 bytes, and
10: - decode these bytes to the equivalent opcode.
11: 
12: The vectors are enforced by the reference Rust encoder (`pathland-core`,
13: `crates/pathland-core/src/conformance.rs`).
14: 
15: Companion catalogs: [PRIMITIVES.md](./PRIMITIVES.md) (views), [MODIFIERS.md](./MODIFIERS.md)

18: implementations depend on them.

24: ```

1: //! Batch wire format: encode/decode opcodes + arena delta into network batches.
2: 
3: use alloc::vec::Vec;
4: use pathland_core::{Event, Frame, Opcode, category, event, meta};
5: 
6: use crate::{BATCH_MAGIC, BATCH_VERSION};
7: 
8: /// Fixed header byte length: magic(4) + version(2) + flags(2) + sequence(4) + opcodeCount(4).
9: pub const BATCH_HEADER: usize = 16;
10: 
11: /// Errors produced while decoding a network batch.
12: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
13: pub enum BatchError {
14:     /// The batch is shorter than the fixed header.
15:     Truncated,
16:     /// The batch magic does not match `BATCH_MAGIC`.
17:     BadMagic,
18:     /// The batch version is not supported.
19:     BadVersion,
20:     /// The opcode payload is truncated (opcodeCount × 16 exceeds the buffer).
21:     BadOpcodeCount,
22:     /// The arena delta length exceeds the remaining buffer.
23:     BadArenaLen,
24: }
25: 
26: /// A decoded network batch: opcodes plus a mirrored arena, exposed as a
27: /// `pathland_core::Frame` so consumers (`RenderTree::apply_frame`) work
28: /// exactly as with shared-memory frames.
29: pub struct Batch<'a> {
30:     frame: Frame<'a>,
31:     sequence: u32,
32:     flags: u16,
33: }
34: 
35: impl<'a> core::fmt::Debug for Batch<'a> {
36:     fn fmt(&self, f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> core::fmt::Result {
37:         f.debug_struct("Batch")
38:             .field("sequence", &self.sequence)
39:             .field("flags", &self.flags)
40:             .field("len", &self.len())
41:             .finish()
42:     }
43: }
44: 
45: impl<'a> Batch<'a> {
46:     /// The opcodes carried by this batch, in order.
47:     pub fn opcodes(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = Opcode> + '_ {
48:         self.frame.opcodes()
49:     }
50: 
51:     /// Number of opcodes in the batch.
52:     pub fn len(&self) -> usize {
53:         self.frame.len()
54:     }
55: 
56:     pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
57:         self.frame.is_empty()
58:     }
59: 
60:     /// The per-stream monotonic message sequence of this batch.
61:     pub fn sequence(&self) -> u32 {
62:         self.sequence
63:     }
64: 
65:     /// Direction flags (see [`crate::direction`]).
66:     pub fn flags(&self) -> u16 {
67:         self.flags
68:     }
69: 
70:     /// View this batch as a `Frame` (the transport seam).
71:     pub fn as_frame(&self) -> &Frame<'a> {
72:         &self.frame
73:     }
74: 
75:     /// Read an arena entry by offset (see `Frame::arena_get`).
76:     pub fn arena_get(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a [u8], pathland_core::ArenaError> {
77:         self.frame.arena_get(offset)
78:     }
79: 
80:     /// Read an arena string by offset.
81:     pub fn arena_str(&self, offset: u32) -> Result<&'a str, pathland_core::ArenaError> {
82:         self.frame.arena_str(offset)
83:     }
84: }

86: /// Serialize one batch from opcodes + an arena delta (bytes appended since the
87: /// previous batch). `sequence` is the per-stream monotonic message sequence
88: /// (increment by one per encoded guest → host batch; `0` for heartbeat/request
89: /// batches). Stateless; see [`BatchEncoder`] for cursor tracking.
90: pub fn encode_batch(
91:     sequence: u32,
92:     flags: u16,
93:     opcodes: &[Opcode],
94:     arena_delta: &[u8],
95: ) -> Vec<u8> {
96:     let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(BATCH_HEADER + opcodes.len() * Opcode::SIZE + arena_delta.len() + 4);
97:     out.extend_from_slice(&BATCH_MAGIC.to_le_bytes());
98:     out.extend_from_slice(&BATCH_VERSION.to_le_bytes());
99:     out.extend_from_slice(&flags.to_le_bytes());
100:     out.extend_from_slice(&sequence.to_le_bytes());
101:     out.extend_from_slice(&(opcodes.len() as u32).to_le_bytes());
102:     for op in opcodes {
103:         out.extend_from_slice(&op.to_bytes());
104:     }
105:     out.extend_from_slice(&(arena_delta.len() as u32).to_le_bytes());
106:     out.extend_from_slice(arena_delta);
107:     out
108: }

110: /// Fields parsed from a batch header + payload regions.
111: struct ParsedBatch<'a> {
112:     flags: u16,
113:     sequence: u32,
114:     opcodes: &'a [u8],
115:     arena_delta: &'a [u8],
116: }
117: 
118: /// Parse a batch header, returning flags, sequence, opcode bytes and arena delta.
119: fn parse(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<ParsedBatch<'_>, BatchError> {
120:     if bytes.len() < BATCH_HEADER {
121:         return Err(BatchError::Truncated);
122:     }
123:     let magic = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[0..4].try_into().unwrap());
124:     if magic != BATCH_MAGIC {
125:         return Err(BatchError::BadMagic);
126:     }
127:     let version = u16::from_le_bytes(bytes[4..6].try_into().unwrap());
128:     if version != BATCH_VERSION {
129:         return Err(BatchError::BadVersion);
130:     }
131:     let flags = u16::from_le_bytes(bytes[6..8].try_into().unwrap());
132:     let sequence = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[8..12].try_into().unwrap());
133:     let opcode_count = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[12..16].try_into().unwrap()) as usize;
134: 
135:     let opcodes_bytes = opcode_count
136:         .checked_mul(Opcode::SIZE)
137:         .ok_or(BatchError::BadOpcodeCount)?;
138:     let opcodes_start = BATCH_HEADER;
139:     let opcodes_end = opcodes_start
140:         .checked_add(opcodes_bytes)
141:         .ok_or(BatchError::BadOpcodeCount)?;
142:     if opcodes_end > bytes.len() {
143:         return Err(BatchError::BadOpcodeCount);
144:     }
145:     let arena_len_pos = opcodes_end;
146:     if arena_len_pos + 4 > bytes.len() {
147:         return Err(BatchError::BadArenaLen);
148:     }
149:     let arena_len = u32::from_le_bytes(bytes[arena_len_pos..arena_len_pos + 4].try_into().unwrap())
150:         as usize;
151:     let arena_start = arena_len_pos + 4;
152:     let arena_end = arena_start
153:         .checked_add(arena_len)
154:         .ok_or(BatchError::BadArenaLen)?;
155:     if arena_end > bytes.len() {
156:         return Err(BatchError::BadArenaLen);
157:     }
158: 
159:     Ok(ParsedBatch {
160:         flags,
161:         sequence,
162:         opcodes: &bytes[opcodes_start..opcodes_end],
163:         arena_delta: &bytes[arena_start..arena_end],
164:     })
165: }

167: /// A streamed network-batch encoder.
168: ///
169: /// Tracks the last arena length so successive batches carry only the bytes
170: /// appended to the bump arena since the previous batch. If the arena is reset
171: /// (shrank — see `META::RESET`), the full used arena is sent and tracking
172: /// restarts.
173: #[derive(Debug, Default)]
174: pub struct BatchEncoder {
175:     last_arena_len: usize,
176: }
177: 
178: impl BatchEncoder {
179:     /// Create a fresh encoder (no arena bytes sent yet).
180:     pub fn new() -> Self {
181:         Self { last_arena_len: 0 }
182:     }
183: 
184:     /// Encode a frame's opcodes plus the arena bytes appended since the last
185:     /// call. `arena_used` is the arena region's used portion (`[0..cursor)`).
186:     ///
187:     /// If the frame contains `META::RESET`, arena tracking restarts (the arena
188:     /// cursor returns to 0) and the full used arena is sent.
189:     pub fn encode(&mut self, sequence: u32, opcodes: &[Opcode], arena_used: &[u8]) -> Vec<u8> {
190:         let reset = opcodes.iter().any(|op| {
191:             op.category() == pathland_core::category::META
192:                 && op.command() == pathland_core::meta::RESET
193:         });
194:         if reset {
195:             self.last_arena_len = 0;
196:         }
197:         let delta = if arena_used.len() >= self.last_arena_len {
198:             &arena_used[self.last_arena_len..]
199:         } else {
200:             // Arena shrank unexpectedly: send the full used arena again.
201:             arena_used
202:         };
203:         let bytes = encode_batch(sequence, crate::direction::GUEST_TO_HOST, opcodes, delta);
204:         self.last_arena_len = arena_used.len();
205:         bytes
206:     }
207: 
208:     /// The arena length already shipped (diagnostics).
209:     pub fn arena_sent(&self) -> usize {
210:         self.last_arena_len
211:     }
212: }

214: /// A streamed network-batch decoder.
215: ///
216: /// Maintains a **mirrored arena**: each batch's arena delta is appended, so
217: /// absolute `arenaRef` offsets resolve exactly as in shared memory. When a
218: /// batch contains `META::RESET`, the mirror is cleared before appending.
219: #[derive(Debug, Default)]
220: pub struct BatchDecoder {
221:     arena: Vec<u8>,
222: }
223: 
224: impl BatchDecoder {
225:     /// Create an empty decoder.
226:     pub fn new() -> Self {
227:         Self { arena: Vec::new() }
228:     }
229: 
230:     /// Decode a batch, appending its arena delta to the mirror.
231:     ///
232:     /// The returned `Batch` borrows `bytes` (opcodes) and this decoder (arena);
233:     /// keep both alive while consuming it.
234:     pub fn decode<'a>(&'a mut self, bytes: &'a [u8]) -> Result<Batch<'a>, BatchError> {
235:         let parsed = parse(bytes)?;
236: 
237:         // A META::RESET in the batch clears the renderer; reset the arena mirror
238:         // to match (offsets restart at 0 after a reset).
239:         let opcode_count = parsed.opcodes.len() / Opcode::SIZE;
240:         let reset = (0..opcode_count).any(|i| {
241:             let op = Opcode::from_bytes(parsed.opcodes[i * Opcode::SIZE..(i + 1) * Opcode::SIZE].try_into().unwrap());
242:             op.category() == pathland_core::category::META
243:                 && op.command() == pathland_core::meta::RESET
244:         });
245:         if reset {
246:             self.arena.clear();
247:         }
248:         self.arena.extend_from_slice(parsed.arena_delta);
249: 
250:         let frame = Frame::from_parts(parsed.opcodes, &self.arena, 0, parsed.opcodes.len());
251:         Ok(Batch {
252:             frame,
253:             sequence: parsed.sequence,
254:             flags: parsed.flags,
255:         })
256:     }
257: 
258:     /// The mirrored arena length (diagnostics).
259:     pub fn arena_len(&self) -> usize {
260:         self.arena.len()
261:     }
262: }

1: //! # pathland-core-transport
2: //!
3: //! How Pathland opcodes are transported from the guest engine to host
4: //! renderers. There are two peer backends:
5: //!
6: //! - **Shared memory** (desktop/native/WASM): the ring buffer + arena in
7: //!   `pathland-core` (`Guest`/`Host`). Zero-copy. This crate treats it as
8: //!   the local transport — no duplication.
9: //! - **Network batch** (SSR → browser): opcodes + string data serialized into
10: //!   **batches**.
11: //!
12: //! There are two network codecs, for two different relationships between the
13: //! producer and the consumer:
14: //!
15: //! - **Self-contained frames** ([`encode_frame`] / [`decode_frame`]) — each
16: //!   batch carries its own string section and `SET_TEXT` references strings by
17: //!   a *relative* offset into that section. The consumer needs **no prior
18: //!   state**: every message is independent. This is the streaming codec used
19: //!   for live deltas over WebSocket.
20: //! - **Arena-delta batches** ([`encode_batch`] / [`BatchEncoder`] /
21: //!   [`BatchDecoder`]) — the batch carries only the bytes *appended* to the
22: //!   arena since the previous batch, and `SET_TEXT` references absolute arena
23: //!   offsets. The consumer mirrors the arena so those offsets stay valid. This
24: //!   mirrors the shared-memory arena over a wire and is the ring-compatible
25: //!   codec (kept for a future WASM/embedded guest).
26: //!
27: //! ## Batch wire format (both codecs share the header)
28: //!
29: //! ```text
30: //! magic "PLPL" (u32 LE) | version (u16) | flags (u16) | sequence (u32)
31: //! | opcodeCount (u32) | opcodes (16 B × opcodeCount) | stringsLen (u32)
32: //! | string bytes (length-prefixed entries: [u32 len][bytes])
33: //! ```
34: //!
35: //! `sequence` is the per-stream monotonic message sequence (incremented once
36: //! per encoded guest → host batch; `0` for heartbeat/request batches). A
37: //! consumer detects lost batches by a sequence gap and recovers with a full
38: //! snapshot — see `spec/OPCODE.md` §Sequence gap detection.
39: //!
40: //! For a self-contained frame the trailing section is that frame's own string
41: //! table; for an arena-delta batch it is the arena bytes appended since the
42: //! last batch.
43: //!
44: //! ## Example (producer)
45: //!
46: //! ```no_run

48: //! use std::time::Duration;
49: //!
50: //! let policy = BatchPolicy::new(Duration::from_millis(4), 1400);
51: //! let mut batcher = Batcher::new(policy);
52: //! let mut encoder = BatchEncoder::new();
53: //!
54: //! // batcher.push_frame(&frame) accumulates opcodes + arena delta;
55: //! // batcher.flush() -> Option<Vec<u8>> produces the serialized batch.
56: //! ```

690: ### SizeThatFits — `SIZE_THAT_FITS` 0x17
691: 
692: A **fit slot**: it shows **one child at a time — the currently selected
693: candidate**. In the **live (delta) form** only that child is ever transmitted:
694: the app owns the candidates (their views never ride the wire) and transmits the
695: **fit query** (`FIT_QUERY`, LIST — the candidates' `minWidth` thresholds,
696: ascending) plus the selected child. In a **full-snapshot emission** (the web SSR
697: first document), every candidate is transmitted as a child — the renderer renders
698: all branches and the browser selects the matching one (see the visibility
699: contract below) so the first paint is already correct. The renderer measures its
700: **own allocated width** (the slot is size-taking — it stretches to its parent's
701: proposal, never hugs, so it always has a well-defined width) and selects the fit
702: **locally**:
703: 
704: > **Fit rule** — the selected index is `max{ i : thresholds[i] ≤ measured
705: > width }` (threshold 0 candidate always qualifies — the fallback); equal
706: > thresholds pick the **lower index**; before the first measure the app renders
707: > the threshold-0 candidate (index 0). The measurement is in **logical points**,
708: > so the pick is identical on every renderer given the same slot width.
709: 
710: The renderer reports its selection back with **`FIT_CHANGED`** ([EVENTS.md](./EVENTS.md))
711: — emitted **once after the first measure, and then only when the derived fit
712: index changes** (a band crossing). It never streams the raw size. The app reacts
713: by swapping the slot's child (a `TREE` delta pair); a selection that maps to the
714: already-shown view re-emits **zero** opcodes. After a **full-snapshot**
715: presentation (all candidates laid out), the first `FIT_CHANGED` is the signal
716: that collapses the slot back to the live single-selected-child form.

720: surface order). In a **full-snapshot emission** the slot's **child order MUST

723: candidate declared first in the DSL but carrying a **higher** `minWidth` is
724: therefore **not** index 0.

726: **Full-snapshot visibility (MUST).** In a full-snapshot emission the renderer
727: MUST show **exactly one** candidate — the one at `index(w)` for the slot's own
728: allocated width `w` — with no JS:

730: - the slot's own width is the query context (each slot is measured
731:   independently);
732: - each candidate is gated behind a marker carrying its `FIT_QUERY` index;

734:   `w ≥ T_i`, makes candidate `i` visible and **hides every candidate `j ≠ i`**;
735:   bands are emitted **ascending** so the highest matching band wins; no band
736:   exists for `T_0`;
737: - the per-candidate **default** (below the first band / no match) is candidate
738:   `0` visible, every other candidate hidden;

742: slot to the live single-selected-child form (the unselected candidates leave as
743: `TREE` deltas) and the renderer removes the full-snapshot gating — the gate
744: markers, the query context, and the band rules — so no CSS gate remains; a
745: `FIT_CHANGED` that maps to the already-shown candidate re-emits **zero** opcodes.

39: /// Allocate into any arena region, using the given header cursor offset.
40: #[inline]
41: pub(crate) fn alloc_at(
42:     data: &mut [u8],
43:     header: &mut [u8],
44:     cursor_off: usize,
45:     bytes: &[u8],
46: ) -> Result<u32, ArenaError> {

48:     let len = bytes.len();

53:     data[cursor..cursor + 4].copy_from_slice(&(len as u32).to_le_bytes());
54:     data[cursor + 4..cursor + needed].copy_from_slice(bytes);
55:     header::set_u32(header, cursor_off, (cursor + needed) as u32);
56:     Ok(cursor as u32)
57: }

# Pathland "proxy view" research report

Note on layout: the emitter you called `pathland-core/engine` now lives in **`lib/rust/crates/pathland-engine`** (`engine.rs`, `node.rs`, `signal.rs`). `pathland-core` holds the pure protocol (`constants.rs`, `opcode.rs`, `arena.rs`, `ring.rs`, `memory.rs`, `lib.rs`). I read both.

## 1. TREE opcode semantics and exact A/B/C layouts

**Spec table** — `spec/OPCODE.md:106-112`:

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Flags |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CREATE_NODE` | `0x01` | nodeId | componentType (u16, low) | 0 | — |
| `DELETE_NODE` | `0x02` | nodeId | 0 | 0 | — |
| `INSERT_CHILD` | `0x03` | parentId | childId | index | — |
| `REMOVE_CHILD` | `0x04` | parentId | childId | 0 | — |
| `MOVE_CHILD` | `0x05` | parentId | childId | newIndex | — |

Append sentinel (`spec/OPCODE.md:110,112`): `index = u32::MAX` (`APPEND`). Constant `pub const APPEND: u32 = u32::MAX;` at `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/constants.rs:772-773`, and command doc comments at `constants.rs:21-33`.

Exact opcode framing (`spec/OPCODE.md:38-65`, `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core/src/opcode.rs:23-38`):
```
[Category: u8][Command: u8][Flags: u16][A: u32][B: u32][C: u32]  // 16 B, little-endian, #[repr(C, packed)]
```

Golden bytes (`spec/CONFORMANCE.md:30-67`):
- `CREATE_NODE` id=1 VSTACK: `01 01 0000 01000000 10000000 00000000`
- `INSERT_CHILD` parent=0 child=1 APPEND: `01 03 0000 00000000 01000000 FFFFFFFF`
- `MOVE_CHILD` parent=1 child=2 newIndex=0: `01 05 0000 01000000 02000000 00000000`

**PARENT/CHILD encoding:** parent in `A`, child in `B`, index in `C`. `REMOVE_CHILD` uses `A=parent, B=child, C=0`. `DELETE_NODE` is node-only (`A`) and deletes the whole subtree (`spec/OPCODE.md:109`).

**ROOT / sentinel conventions — there is NO root id in the protocol, and no reserved node id.**
- The consumer discovers the root structurally as **"the single node without a parent."** `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-gtk/src/host.rs:277-280`:
  ```rust
  /// The root node: the single node without a parent.
  pub fn root(&self) -> Option<&HostNode> {
      self.nodes.values().find(|n| n.parent.is_none())
  }
  ```
  Same in the native flat-world host: `lib/rust/crates/pathland-view-native/src/lib.rs:220-222`.
- **No `INSERT_CHILD` ever targets an implicit root.** Both emitters create the root with `CREATE_NODE` and never insert it into a parent:
  - Rust: `engine.rs:445-451` — `guest.create_node(node.id, …)` then `if let Some(p) = parent { guest.insert_child(p, node.id, …) }`; the recursive root call passes `parent=None` (`engine.rs:121`).
  - Java: `Emitter.java:273-298` — emits `createNode(root.id,…)` then inserts only *children* (`sink.insertChild(node.id, child.id, -1)` at line 296).
- Node id `0` is **not reserved**. `HostNode::default()` itself is `id: 0` (`host.rs:68-81`), and `Node::id` is documented "0 until `assign_ids`" (`pathland-engine/src/node.rs:30`). Real emitters just start the root at **1** (see §2), so 0 is de-facto unused but not a sentinel.
- Conformance vector 2 (`CONFORMANCE.md:43-54`) uses `parent=0`, but that is a **standalone byte-layout example**, not an implicit root: it is independent of vector 1 (which was `CREATE_NODE id=1`), so `0` is just an arbitrary payload there. No production code emits `INSERT_CHILD` with parent 0.

## 2. Node id allocation — per emitter, not global; collisions are possible

**Ids are plain `u32`** (`spec/OPCODE.md:73`). The protocol defines no allocator, no global registry, and no reserved ranges.

- **Rust:** `assign_ids(root, next: &mut u32)` assigns **pre-order, root first**, and the caller supplies the starting counter — `lib/rust/crates/pathland-engine/src/node.rs:275-285`:
  ```rust
  pub fn assign_ids(root: &mut Node, next: &mut u32) {
      root.id = *next; *next += 1;
      for child in &mut root.children { assign_ids(child, next); }
  }
  ```
  Every call site starts at `1` (demo/main `pathland-render-gtk-demo/src/main.rs:119`, README `lib/rust/README.md:104`, all tests). So the Rust id space is **per-tree/per-emitter**, not global.
- **Java:** `Emitter` owns its own counter, reset to `1` per mount — `Emitter.java:59` (`private int nextId = 1;`), `Emitter.java:119-120` (`nextId = 1; assignIds(tree);`), `Emitter.java:197-202`:
  ```java
  private void assignIds(PathlandNode node) {
      node.id = nextId++;
      for (PathlandNode child : node.children) assignIds(child);
  }
  ```
  The root gets id **1**; asserted by `EmitterTest.java:48` (`assertEquals(1, result.rootId());`). Structural reconcile allocates new ids from the same `nextId++` (`Emitter.java:567, 666`).
- **Native C-ABI flat world:** ids are entirely **host-supplied** (`pathland_native_create_node(host, id, component)`), see `pathland-view-native/src/lib.rs:74-77` and `capi.rs`.
- **Collisions:** **Yes, two independent emitters collide.** Both Rust and Java start at `1`, and there is no namespacing. Concretely:
  - GTK renderer stores nodes in a flat `HashMap<u32, HostNode>` (`host.rs:87`) and `CREATE_NODE` does `self.nodes.entry(id).or_default()` (`host.rs:176-182`) — a colliding id silently **merges/reuses** the existing entry (component type overwritten, text/properties mixed).
  - DOM client keeps a **document-global** `Map<number, Node> byId`, built from `document.querySelectorAll("[data-pathland-id]")` (`lib/typescript/src/index.ts:103-106`), keyed by `op.a` on `CREATE_NODE` (`apply.ts:474-485`) — a second tree's id reuses the first tree's element.
  - The CSS container name for `SizeThatFits` is derived from the node id (`pf-<id>`, see §6), so collisions also break container queries.

**Conclusion for the proxy plan:** any foreign subtree injected into A's stream MUST have its node ids remapped to a disjoint range (or offset) inside A's emitter before emission. The protocol gives you no automatic namespacing.

## 3. PLPL network batch format, frames, and META commands

**Single wire format, one shared header** — `spec/OPCODE.md:660-684`; Rust `lib/rust/crates/pathland-core-transport/src/batch.rs:86-108`; Java `FrameCodec.java:16-62, 337-343`; TS `plpl.ts:28-77`:

```
offset 0   magic    u32 LE = 0x504C504C ("PLPL")
offset 4   version  u16 LE = 1
offset 6   flags    u16 LE   (0x0000 guest→host, 0x0001 host→guest)
offset 8   sequence u32 LE   (per-stream monotonic; 0 for heartbeat/request)
offset 12  opcodeCount u32 LE
offset 16  opcodes: opcodeCount × 16 B
then       stringsLen u32 LE
then       string/arena bytes (length-prefixed entries `[u32 len][bytes]`)
```
Header is exactly 16 bytes: `BATCH_HEADER: usize = 16` (`batch.rs:8-9`). Magic/version/direction constants: `pathland-core-transport/src/lib.rs:80-91` (`BATCH_MAGIC=0x504C_504C`, `BATCH_VERSION=1`, `direction::GUEST_TO_HOST=0x0000`, `HOST_TO_GUEST=0x0001`); Java mirrors them at `FrameCodec.java:34-38`.

**Sections:** there is exactly **one trailing byte section**, whose meaning is codec-dependent — there is no multi-section "frames/events/strings" layout:
- **Self-contained frame codec** (`encode_frame`/`decode_frame`, `batch.rs:364-405`; Java `FrameCodec.encodeFrame/decodeFrame`, `FrameCodec.java:42-68`): the trailing bytes are the frame's **own string table**, and string/list operands use **relative offsets** into it. No prior state required.
- **Arena-delta codec** (`encode_batch`/`BatchEncoder`/`BatchDecoder`, `batch.rs:86-262`): the trailing bytes are only the **arena bytes appended since the previous batch**; string operands use **absolute arena offsets** and the consumer keeps a mirrored arena (`BatchDecoder`, `batch.rs:219-261`).
- **Host→guest events** reuse the same header with `flags=HOST_TO_GUEST`; `TEXT_CHANGED`/`NAVIGATE` strings ride the same trailing section via **relative** offsets (`encode_events`/`decode_events`, `batch.rs:264-344`; `FrameCodec.encodeEvents`, `FrameCodec.java:187-245`).

**Frame delimiting:** a batch is the **network unit, not a frame**. There is no per-frame delimiter inside a batch; opcodes are delimited only by `opcodeCount`. Several emit-pass frames may coalesce into one batch (`spec/OPCODE.md:676-679`). On the shared-memory ring, frame boundaries are detected via the header `frameCount` (`spec/OPCODE.md:517-523`). Batching policy: flush at 4 ms or 1400 bytes, first wins (`spec/OPCODE.md:686-695`; `batching.rs:16-43`). `META::RESET` inside a batch clears the mirrored arena before appending (`batch.rs:190-206, 237-248`).

**META category commands** — `spec/OPCODE.md:404-436`, constants `constants.rs:108-140`:

| Command | Value | A | B | C | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `RESET` | `0x01` | 0 | 0 | 0 | Host clears rendered output + mirrored arena |
| `ENVIRONMENT` | `0x02` | fieldId (u16 low) | field value | 0 | One platform env field (host→guest) |
| `RESYNC` | `0x03` | 0 | 0 | 0 | Host requests full snapshot (host→guest) |
| `PING` | `0x04` | 0 | 0 | 0 | Heartbeat probe (guest→host; network only) |
| `PONG` | `0x05` | 0 | 0 | 0 | Heartbeat reply (host→guest; network only) |

Environment field ids (`constants.rs:132-140`): `VIEWPORT_WIDTH=0x0001` (f32 in B), `VIEWPORT_HEIGHT=0x0002` (f32 in B), `ROUTE=0x0003` (string offset in B). Java encodes them at `FrameCodec.java:105-129` (route string at relative offset 0); decodes at `FrameCodec.java:164-185`. `META::RESYNC` request batch builder: Rust `encode_resync()` (`batch.rs:379-389`), Java `FrameCodec.encodeResync()` (`FrameCodec.java:78-85`) — both a single RESYNC opcode, `HOST_TO_GUEST`, sequence 0, empty string section. RESYNC semantics: host asks for a full snapshot; guest answers with a full TREE+PARAMETER mount batch (`spec/OPCODE.md:410`).

## 4. Id spaces

- **Node id space: full `u32`** (`spec/OPCODE.md:73`), carried in `A` (and `B` for child in INSERT/REMOVE/MOVE). No reserved values; no documented upper bound beyond `u32`.
- **PARAMETER `A` field is the node id (`u32`)** — `spec/OPCODE.md:122`; `SET_PROPERTY A=nodeId`. So the "PARAMETER A field" is the same u32 node-id space, not a separate one.
- **Property id space: `u16`** (0x0000–0xFFFF), packed into the **low two bytes of `B`**; the **value type is the high byte of the 16-bit upper half**: `B = (valueType << 16) | propertyId` (`spec/OPCODE.md:127-131`; `FrameOpcodeSink.java:85`; `host.rs:220-222`). So bits 16–23 = valueType (u8), bits 24–31 unused/reserved. Example SPACING: `B = 0x00040001` (`CONFORMANCE.md:69-82`).
- **Component type space: `u16`** (low half of `B` in `CREATE_NODE`) — `spec/OPCODE.md:74,108`; ranges `0x01–0x0F` drawing, `0x10–0x1F` layout, `0x20–0x2F` controls, `0x7F` COMMENT (`constants.rs:224-316`).
- **Value types: u8** (`constants.rs:209-222`): `U8=1,U32=2,I32=3,F32=4,STRING=5,ENUM=6,COLOR=7,DESIGN_TOKEN=8,LIST=9`.
- **Other id spaces:** category/command are `u8` (`Category==0` and `Command==0` reserved; categories `0x80–0xFF` are "custom/extended" — `spec/OPCODE.md:78-82`); design-token keys are strings (not numeric); `EVENT_LISTENERS`/`BORDER_EDGES` are `u32` bitmasks (`constants.rs:157-206`).

I searched `spec/` and all of `lib/` case-insensitively for `proxy`, `portal`, `iframe`, `embed*`, `remote view`, `host view`, `foreign tree`, `subtree injection`, `nested tree`, `foreign`. Findings:

- **No protocol/docs mention of a proxy view, portal, remote/foreign subtree injection, or nesting another server's tree.** Nothing in `spec/OPCODE.md`, `PRIMITIVES.md`, `MODIFIERS.md`, `EVENTS.md`, `LAYOUT.md`, `DSL.md`, `TOKENS.md`, `CONFORMANCE.md`, `ICONS.md`.

**Interpretation:** a proxy/portal view would be a **new primitive** (new `component_type`, likely in a free range, or a new category using `0x80–0xFF`) — the protocol has no existing concept for it. There is also no message that says "these nodes came from server B," no namespace field on `CREATE_NODE`, and no root/session identity in the opcode stream. The only cross-instance mechanisms present are transport-level: `sequence` gap detection + `META::RESYNC` full snapshot (`spec/OPCODE.md:697-725`), and `META::RESET` to clear a renderer (`spec/OPCODE.md:408`).

## 6. SizeThatFits / container queries and node ids

The node id **is** used directly as the CSS container name and DOM identity, so it must be **unique within the rendered document**:

- The HTML renderer emits, for a multi-candidate `SIZE_THAT_FITS` slot, `container-type:inline-size; container-name:pf-{id}` where `{id}` is the node id — `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/src/lib.rs:1354`:
  ```
  "display:flex;…;container-type:inline-size;container-name:pf-{id};{css}{derived}"
  ```
- Band rules are generated as `@container pf-{id} (min-width: {t}px) { … }` and match descendants by `[data-pathland-id="{id}"]` — `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-html/src/lib.rs:115-148` (esp. lines 132, 138, 142).
- The DOM client removes a slot's rules by regex `@container pf-${slotId}\b` (word-boundary so slot `1` never matches slot `10`) — `lib/typescript/src/apply.ts:1498-1511`; it also manipulates `data-pathland-id`, `data-pathland-fit-cands`, and `data-pathland-fit-cand` wrappers (`apply.ts:1445-1490`).
- Candidate-identity contract: the slot's child order equals `FIT_QUERY` order; each candidate is gated by index (`spec/PRIMITIVES.md:690-764`, esp. 718-739). `FIT_QUERY` is the `LIST` property `0x1039` (`spec/OPCODE.md:230`); `FIT_CHANGED` is event `0x13` targeting the slot's node id (`spec/EVENTS.md:279,286-291`; `constants.rs:105`).
- The renderer reports the selected fit index **keyed by node id** (`sink.fitChanged(op.a(), …)`; Java routes `FIT_CHANGED` through `fitInputs` keyed by `node.id`, `Emitter.java:54`, `PathlandNode.fitInput`).

**Consequence for a proxy view:** because `pf-<id>` and `[data-pathland-id="<id>"]` are document-global, two independently-numbered emitters (each starting at 1) will collide — a `SizeThatFits` slot in A and one in the embedded B-subtree could share an id, and the band rules would cross-contaminate. The proxy must allocate a disjoint id range for the injected subtree (and strings must be rebased, because self-contained frames use *relative* string offsets within one string section — `spec/OPCODE.md:338-340`, `batch.rs:364-377`, `plpm.ts readString`).

## Additional concrete facts relevant to the plan

- **Root id in practice is `1`** in both stacks (Java `Emitter.java:59,119-120` + `EmitterTest.java:48`; Rust callers always pass `&mut 1`), but this is a convention, not a protocol constant. The consumer must not assume 1 — it finds the parentless node (`host.rs:277-280`).
- **Two independent emitters collide** at id 1 onward; a `CREATE_NODE` on an existing id is merged (GTK `host.rs:179`, DOM `apply.ts:474-485`).
- **The proxy must either remap ids or extend the protocol** (new primitive + namespace/offset, or a host-reserved range). There is currently no id offset/namespace field anywhere in the 16-byte opcode.
- **Frames and batches**: a batch has one trailing byte section; self-contained frames use relative string offsets, arena-delta batches use absolute offsets with a mirrored arena (`batch.rs:167-262`). Events are host→guest batches with `flags=0x0001` and relative strings (`batch.rs:264-344`).
- **META extensions** are field families, not new commands (`ENVIRONMENT` pattern, `spec/OPCODE.md:414-436`), and categories `0x80–0xFF` are reserved for custom/extended use (`spec/OPCODE.md:82`) — the only protocol-level hook for a future proxy/portal primitive.
